name: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time.
shortDescription: Find length of longest consecutive sequence

methods.name: computeWithHashSet
methods.label: Hash set

methods.name: computeWithRecursion
methods.label: Recursion

methods.name: computeWithSorting
methods.label: Sorting

explanation.idea: A run of consecutive numbers has exactly one start: a number whose predecessor (x − 1) isn't in the data. Only count upward from those starts, so each number is visited a constant number of times.
explanation.analogy: Finding the longest chain of house numbers on a street: only start counting at a house whose left neighbour's number is missing, then walk right until the numbers stop.

computeWithHashSet.summary: Put all numbers in a set; from each sequence start, count up.
steps: Add every number to a set (this also removes duplicates).
For each number, skip it unless num − 1 is absent: it isn't the start of a run.
From a start, keep checking num + 1, num + 2… and count the run.
computeWithHashSet.timeWhy: Each number is the start check once and is counted in at most one run, so the total work is about 2n.

computeWithRecursion.summary: Same starts, but the run length is counted recursively.
steps: Build the set and find the starts as above.
findSequenceLength(set, num) returns 0 if num isn't present, else 1 + the length from num + 1.
computeWithRecursion.timeWhy: The same visits as the iterative version.
computeWithRecursion.spaceWhy: The set, plus a call stack as deep as the longest run (a run of a million numbers would overflow).

computeWithSorting.summary: Sort, then walk and count runs, ignoring repeated values.
steps: If the next value is previous + 1, extend the run.
If it's equal, skip it (duplicates don't break a run).
Otherwise close the run and start a new one.
computeWithSorting.timeWhy: Sorting dominates; this breaks the O(n) requirement.
computeWithSorting.spaceWhy: Sort stack space; changes the input.

pitfalls: Counting up from every number, not just starts, makes it O(n²).
Forgetting duplicates in the sorted version ([1, 2, 2, 3] is a run of 3).
interview: The key sentence: "only start counting where num − 1 is missing". Then argue why that makes it linear.
Mention the sorting version as the simpler O(n log n) baseline.
